rows.description: A child realises that a sibling who broke a toy was scared and not mean. Perspective-taking at this age is real but effortful and often fades under anger.
A teenager quarrelling with a parent can only see their side, though calm afterwards they understand the parent's fear. Emotion narrows the view, and wisdom includes waiting until it widens.
A toddler shakes the head to say no, often before speaking clearly, showing refusal or a wish for control. It is meaningful communication that adults can respond to with respect.
A child lowers the head after doing something wrong or when embarrassed, showing shame or fear. Kind correction helps the child learn without feeling worthless.

rows.subtype: Bowing the head in respect and mourning [Expressing]
rows.description: An adult bows the head at a funeral, prayer or a formal greeting to show respect or grief. The meaning shifts with setting and tradition, and observers follow local custom.

A child hears a tut or a click of the tongue meaning disapproval in some places, or a sound of sympathy or a yes in others. Culture and tone change the meaning, so a listener should not jump to conclusions.

A teenager snorts or clears the throat, and peers may read it as mockery, warning or a real need. The sound is ambiguous; a child with a cold or a tic should not be blamed, and asking calmly avoids unfair conclusions.

A young adult whistles or hums for calm or joy, but whistling at a person in public can be unwelcome harassment. Recognising when a sound crosses into disrespect helps, and anyone targeted may leave and report it.
A child shares a toy with the friend who shared last time, and refuses the one who never does. Early fairness is expressed as "you did for me, I do for you".
A child notes who helped whom, and objects loudly to unequal splits, even when they would receive the extra. A sense that fairness matters is emerging, sometimes rigidly.
A child holds the shoulders tight before saying something in class, showing nervousness. Slow breaths and a friendly nod from the teacher help.
A teenager rolls the shoulders to release tension before a match or exam, or holds them tense when anxious. Noticing and releasing them is a useful calming tool.
A young professional holds tension in the shoulders during deadlines, and stretching or brief breaks help. Colleagues may read tight shoulders as irritation when it is strain.
A school-age child suggests how to play a game or advises a friend on a problem. Advice that is not asked for can feel bossy, so asking would you like ideas is kinder.
A young adult leading a team or lab gives clear directions with the reason and expected result. Commanding without explanation may achieve compliance but weaken trust.
